summary.text: The sixth term \(b=(2^{171}+1)/9\) satisfies \(b\equiv3\pmod{18}\), as \(2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{162}\). Since \(19\mid171\) and \(2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}\), it follows that \(2^b+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), so the required division by \(171\) at the seventh step is not exact.

full_proof.text:
Let the sequence be defined for as long as the recurrence produces integers by
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
For the quotient defining \(a(n)\) to be an integer, it is necessary and sufficient that
\[
a(n-2)\mid 2^{a(n-1)}+1.
\]
We will show that all the terms through \(a(6)\) are integers, but that this divisibility fails when one tries to define \(a(7)\).

The first few applications of the recurrence give
\[
 a(3)=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,
\]
\[
 a(4)=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,
\]
and
\[
 a(5)=\frac{2^9+1}{3}=\frac{513}{3}=171.
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
 a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
We need more than merely the fact that this is an integer: the key information is its residue modulo \(18\). We now prove
\[
 a(6)\equiv 3\pmod {18}.
\]

First compute \(2^{171}\) modulo \(162\). Since \(\varphi(81)=54\) and \(2\) is relatively prime to \(81\), Euler's theorem gives
\[
2^{54}\equiv 1\pmod {81}.
\]
Because \(171=3\cdot54+9\), it follows that
\[
2^{171}=(2^{54})^3 2^9\equiv 2^9=512\equiv 26\pmod {81}.
\]
Both \(2^{171}\) and \(26\) are even. Their difference is therefore divisible by \(2\), as well as by \(81\). Since \(2\) and \(81\) are coprime, their difference is divisible by \(162\). Hence
\[
2^{171}\equiv 26\pmod {162}.
\]
Adding \(1\) gives
\[
2^{171}+1\equiv 27\pmod {162}.
\]
Consequently there is an integer \(t\) such that
\[
2^{171}+1=162t+27=9(18t+3).
\]
This first shows that \(9\mid 2^{171}+1\), so \(a(6)\) really is an integer. Dividing the displayed equality by \(9\), we obtain
\[
a(6)=18t+3,
\]
and therefore
\[
a(6)\equiv3\pmod {18}.
\]
(In decimal notation this integer is
\(332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\), but its residue modulo \(18\), rather than its full expansion, is what is needed.)

Now consider the recurrence step that would define \(a(7)\). Its denominator is
\[
a(5)=171=9\cdot19.
\]
We examine its numerator \(2^{a(6)}+1\) modulo \(19\). Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod {19},
\]
since \(19\) is prime and does not divide \(2\). From \(a(6)=18t+3\), we therefore get
\[
2^{a(6)}=2^{18t+3}=(2^{18})^t2^3\equiv 1^t\cdot8=8\pmod {19}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{a(6)}+1\equiv 9\pmod {19}.
\]
In particular, \(19\nmid 2^{a(6)}+1\). Since \(19\mid171\), divisibility by \(171\) would imply divisibility by \(19\). Therefore
\[
171\nmid 2^{a(6)}+1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(5)\nmid 2^{a(6)}+1.
\]
Hence
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{a(5)}
     =\frac{2^{a(6)}+1}{171}
\]
is not an integer. The recurrence thus fails the required integrality condition at \(n=7\), disproving the conjecture that every term is an integer.
